what_it_is: A generalized version of the retail media network model, applied to any company that owns first-party transaction data and customer attention beyond classic retailers: marketplaces, travel platforms, fintechs, delivery and rideshare apps. CMN lets these companies sell ad space to external brands based on their purchase or behavioral data.
why_marketers_care: Commerce media is expanding well past Amazon/Walmart-style retail media. Marketers now need to evaluate a much wider set of CMN partners (airlines, banks, delivery apps, ride-hailing) as new first-party-data ad inventory, and budgets are shifting there because of stronger ROAS versus open web display.
example: Forbes (April 2026): "Commerce Media Networks: The Next Frontier In Brand Advertising," describing CMNs as the generalization of RMNs to marketplaces, travel, delivery and financial platforms.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term in circulation since roughly 2023 among adtech vendors, but reached broad marketer trade-press mainstream in 2025-2026 as McKinsey and eMarketer projected commerce media growing 20%+ CAGR through 2027.
notes: No em-dashes used. Distinguish from RMN/RMP already in dictionary; CMN is the broader umbrella term.

what_it_is: A commerce media network built by a bank, card network, payment platform, or fintech (e.g., Chase, Mastercard, PayPal) that monetizes its transaction-level, high-intent consumer data by selling advertising to brands.
why_marketers_care: FMNs give advertisers access to purchase-behavior data that is arguably richer than retailer data (income signals, cross-category spend). eMarketer projects FMN ad spend growing at roughly 107% CAGR from 2024-2026 in the US, making it a fast-emerging budget line for performance and brand marketers.
example: Mastercard Commerce Media launched October 2, 2025, citing reach across more than 160 billion transactions processed in 2024 and 500 million enrolled consumers (Digiday, eMarketer coverage).
first_seen_or_mainstream: Became a distinct, named category in trade press through 2025, with eMarketer publishing a dedicated "Financial Media Networks Explainer" and forecast in 2025.
notes: Directly answers the brief's request for commerce media acronyms beyond RMN/RMP.

what_it_is: A TikTok Shop live-commerce efficiency metric: total GMV (Gross Merchandise Value) generated per 1,000 livestream views. It is TikTok's equivalent of CPM but measured in sales output rather than ad cost.
why_marketers_care: GPM is the primary metric TikTok Shop sellers, creators, and agencies use to judge whether a LIVE session is actually converting, and TikTok's algorithm uses GPM signals to decide how much extra reach to give a livestream. It matters directly to any brand or agency running TikTok Shop LIVE selling, including in Turkiye/MEA markets.
example: TikTok Shop Seller Academy course "GPM Video Guide" and multiple TikTok Shop analytics guides cite benchmark ranges of roughly $80-250 GPM for most consumer categories, $300+ for beauty.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Became standard shorthand among TikTok Shop sellers and agencies through 2024-2025 as TikTok Shop LIVE commerce scaled in the US and Southeast Asia.
notes: TikTok Shop primary source (Seller Academy) confirms the metric exists but did not return the full definition text in the fetch; definition corroborated by two independent marketing sources.

what_it_is: A hybrid technical role blending RevOps, marketing ops, data engineering, and AI/prompt engineering to build and automate the systems (enrichment, outbound, lead routing, AI agents) that power a company's marketing and sales motion.
why_marketers_care: It signals a structural shift in B2B marketing organizations: technical GTM builders are now sitting alongside marketers, and marketing leaders are increasingly expected to hire or partner with this role to run AI-driven outbound and demand programs.
example: ZoomInfo ("What Is GTM Engineering? The Complete 2026 Guide") reports the title first appeared on Google Trends in April 2025, with GTM engineer job listings up roughly 205% between 2024 and 2025 and over 3,000 open LinkedIn roles by January 2026.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Emerged as a named role in 2024, went mainstream on LinkedIn/B2B hiring in 2025-2026.
notes: GTM itself is not a new acronym, but its use as a standalone role/title (GTM Engineer, GTM Engineering) is the newly mainstream unit here.

what_it_is: An evolution of ABM (Account-Based Marketing) that extends personalized, coordinated engagement across the full customer lifecycle (marketing, sales, onboarding, customer success, renewal), not just acquisition.
why_marketers_care: B2B marketing orgs are being asked to justify ABM spend against retention and expansion revenue, not just pipeline; ABX reframes account strategy as a shared, cross-functional discipline, which changes how B2B marketers plan 2025-2026 GTM programs.
example: Heinz Marketing, "Planning Your 2025 ABX Go-To-Market Approach," and Content Marketing Institute's "ABX: Take Account-Based Marketing Back to a Better Future."
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term circulated from roughly 2021 but became a standard planning framework in B2B marketing content through 2024-2025.
notes: ABM itself is not in the existing dictionary; noted here only as reference context, not claimed as a separate new entry.

what_it_is: Organic content (LinkedIn posts, short-form video, behind-the-scenes clips) created by a company's own employees rather than its marketing team or paid influencers.
why_marketers_care: As UGC and influencer costs rise and audiences distrust polished brand content, marketers are formalizing employee advocacy/EGC programs; Forbes and multiple 2025 sources report EGC posts get several times more engagement and reach than branded posts.
example: Forbes Agency Council (Feb 2025), "The Hidden Power Of Employee-Generated Content," and multiple 2025 agency guides positioning EGC as a named content category alongside UGC.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Named and tracked as a distinct content category through 2025 trade press (Forbes, Metricool, DSMN8).
notes: CGC already exists in dictionary (likely Creator-Generated Content); EGC is distinct (employees, not creators).

what_it_is: A C-suite role that owns growth across the funnel (acquisition, conversion, retention) by blending marketing, product, and data functions, distinct from a CMO (brand/demand) or CRO (near-term revenue execution).
why_marketers_care: It reshapes marketing org charts: in many companies the CMO now reports into, or is replaced by, a CGO. Secondary sources citing a 2024 Gartner report state nearly 40% of Fortune 500 companies now have a CGO, up from about 15% two years earlier.
example: Cowen Partners, "All About Chief Growth Officers (CGOs)"; multiple 2025 executive-search articles document CGO appointments replacing or absorbing CMO scope.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Adoption accelerated markedly in 2024-2025 per the cited Gartner-sourced statistic.
notes: The 40%/15% Gartner figure is cited by secondary sources, not verified against a primary Gartner document; treat the precise numbers as reported-not-confirmed.

what_it_is: A unified operations function aligning marketing, sales, and customer success processes, data, and systems around shared revenue goals, replacing siloed MarketingOps/SalesOps/CS Ops teams.
why_marketers_care: RevOps has crossed from early-adopter to majority practice inside this window: secondary reporting citing 2025 data states 60.2% of companies now have an officially defined RevOps function, up from about 7% a year earlier, directly changing who marketing reports to and how marketing is measured.
example: Gartner's original 2021 prediction (75% of high-growth companies deploying RevOps by 2025/2026) is now widely cited as having materially played out, per multiple 2025 RevOps trend reports.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term coined earlier (~2019-2021) but crossed into majority adoption and routine marketing-org vocabulary in 2024-2025.
notes: The 7%-to-60.2% adoption jump is reported by a secondary source (CETDIGIT/other blogs), not a primary Gartner or research-firm publication; flagged as reported-not-independently-confirmed.

what_it_is: Low-quality websites engineered primarily to sell ad inventory (via clickbait, excessive ad load, content farms) rather than to serve readers; formally defined by a coalition of ANA, 4A's, WFA, and ISBA.
why_marketers_care: MFA has become a standard line item in brand-safety and media-quality audits; the ANA's Programmatic Transparency Benchmark now tracks MFA exposure across advertisers, and 2024-2025 reports (Adalytics, ANA) show ad tech and agencies still routing meaningful spend to MFA inventory despite crackdown pledges, so marketers must actively screen for it.
example: ANA, "Programmatic Transparency: Made for Advertising Websites Are Too 'Good' to Be True" (2024); Marketing Dive, "Ad tech, agency firms continue to prop up MFAs despite crackdown pledges."
first_seen_or_mainstream: Formally defined September 2023 (just before the window), but became a mainstream, actively monitored marketer concern through 2024-2025 media-quality reporting.
notes: Origin date (Sept 2023) is technically just outside the Sept 2024-Sept 2026 window; included because mainstream marketer awareness and active benchmarking clearly intensified within the window. Flag for editor judgment on the boundary.

what_it_is: EU regulation governing online platforms, including specific transparency and targeting rules for digital advertising (ad parameter disclosure, ban on targeting minors, restrictions on sensitive-data-based targeting).
why_marketers_care: Fully applicable since February 17, 2024, the DSA now directly constrains how marketers run targeted and programmatic campaigns on any platform reaching EU users, with fines up to 6% of global annual turnover; relevant to any Turkiye/MEA marketer running EU-facing campaigns.
example: European Data Protection Board's Guidelines 3/2025 (September 2025) on how the DSA and GDPR interact for advertising compliance.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Fully applicable Feb 2024; enforcement and marketer-facing compliance guidance intensified through 2025.
notes: Law itself dates to 2022, but its "fully applicable" date (Feb 2024) and marketer-facing compliance mainstreaming fall inside or right at the edge of the window.

what_it_is: EU directive requiring large companies to publish detailed, audited sustainability data, which in turn forces marketing/communications teams to back up any environmental or social claims with reportable evidence.
why_marketers_care: It is now a direct constraint on sustainability marketing and green claims: companies were expected to provide audit-ready data behind sustainability claims by end of 2025, and parallel EU green-claims enforcement (Green Claims Code, Greenwashing Directive) is escalating through 2025-2026, with fines up to 10% of turnover in the UK's parallel regime.
example: KPMG Ireland, "Top Sustainability Themes" briefings and multiple 2025 marketing-compliance guides tie CSRD directly to what brands can claim in advertising.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Enforcement and marketer-facing compliance deadlines landed through 2024-2025.
notes: Directive predates the window (adopted 2022) but its marketer-facing enforcement/compliance mainstreaming is squarely 2024-2026.

what_it_is: Amazon's privacy-safe data clean room where advertisers can analyze ad performance, build audience segments, and track cross-format customer journeys using pseudonymized Amazon signals plus their own data.
why_marketers_care: In 2025 Amazon opened AMC access to any advertiser running Sponsored Products, Sponsored Display, Sponsored Brands, or Sponsored TV, without requiring a DSP relationship or separate registration, sharply widening who can use clean-room measurement.
example: Adweek, "Any Seller Buying Sponsored Product Ads on Amazon Can Now Use Amazon's Clean Room" (2025).
first_seen_or_mainstream: AMC launched in 2021, but its access expansion to all advertisers in 2025 is what made it broadly mainstream for mid-market marketers.
notes: Product itself predates the window (2021); flagged because the acronym's mainstream reach among marketers is the 2025 access expansion, not the product launch.

what_it_is: An executive who unifies marketing, sales, e-commerce/merchandising, and customer experience under one P&L-owning role, increasingly common in retail and CPG companies.
why_marketers_care: Many CCOs are promoted from marketing leadership, and the role often sits above or absorbs CMO scope; JM Search and Knownwell both describe the CCO moving from "puzzlement to imperative" in 2024-2025, changing who marketing reports to.
example: Walgreens Boots Alliance named Rachael Vegas Chief Commercial Officer in 2025; Dexcom named Jon Coleman CCO in March 2025 over global sales, marketing, and customer experience.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Role existed earlier, but adoption and marketing-org visibility accelerated in 2024-2025 per multiple executive-search firms.
notes: CCO has competing expansions in the wild: Chief Commercial Officer (marketing-relevant one used here), Chief Customer Officer, Chief Content Officer, and Chief Compliance Officer. Only the Chief Commercial Officer sense is documented here.

what_it_is: An influencer with recognized authority/expertise in a category (originally medical/scientific, now beauty, tech, lifestyle), distinguished from a KOC (Key Opinion Consumer, an everyday user whose reviews read as authentic).
why_marketers_care: KOL/KOC terminology, long standard in Chinese social commerce (Xiaohongshu, Douyin), is now crossing into Western marketing vocabulary as TikTok Shop and cross-border commerce push agencies and brands outside China to adopt the same tiered creator strategy (KOL for reach, KOC for social proof), directly relevant to Turkiye/MEA marketers running cross-border TikTok Shop campaigns.
example: Reacherapp and multiple TikTok Shop growth guides explicitly frame "KOL" as the term Western brands scaling on TikTok Shop need to learn, importing it from the China playbook.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Long-established in China; crossover into mainstream Western/global marketer vocabulary accelerated in 2024-2025 alongside TikTok Shop growth.
notes: KOC already exists in the dictionary as "Key Opinion Consumer" (#257); KOL is its natural, closely related, and currently missing counterpart term.

what_it_is: Meta's ad product (rebranded publicly as "Collaborative Ads") that lets a brand and a retail/marketplace partner co-run Facebook/Instagram ads using the retailer's catalog and audience data, directing clicks to the retailer's product pages.
why_marketers_care: It is a direct bridge between social advertising and commerce/retail media, and its retailer network keeps expanding into quick-commerce and Turkiye/MEA-relevant marketplaces (Trendyol lists CPAS as one of its four core ad models). Meta highlighted CPAS as a growth driver for quick commerce in a December 2025 post.
example: Meta, "How Meta's Collaborative Ads Are Fueling Quick Commerce Boom In India" (about.fb.com, December 2025); Trendyol seller guides list CPAS (Facebook/Instagram) alongside product and store ads as a core advertising model.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Product launched earlier (around 2019-2020) but expanded materially into quick-commerce and additional regional marketplace partnerships in 2025.
notes: Product predates the window; included because its retailer footprint and marketer relevance (including Trendyol in the Turkiye market) expanded materially within 2024-2026.

what_it_is: A managed, modular, API-first technology and services model that lets a retailer stand up a full retail media business (ad serving, campaign management, reporting) without building it in-house.
why_marketers_care: As mid-size and regional retailers (relevant to Turkiye/MEA markets) try to launch their own retail media networks, RMaaS vendors are the fastest path to market; it is a category marketers evaluating new RMN partners will increasingly encounter.
example: Adhese, "Adhese launches Retail Media as a Service (RMaaS), strengthening leadership team with two key hires" (2025).
first_seen_or_mainstream: Emerged as a named vendor category in 2024-2025.
notes: Weakest-sourced item in this set: primarily documented via one vendor's own announcement (Adhese) plus a competing RMAAS.net product name; not yet confirmed as an industry-standard term via independent trade press (Digiday/eMarketer searches did not surface independent RMaaS coverage). Flag for editor to verify with a second independent source before publishing, or downgrade to notes-only.
